# Phase Three — Critique, Safeguards, Verification

The Awtsmoos renews every instant, so stale assumptions cannot lead;
Awtsmoos.com must prove the calendar path in code, in tests, and in the reader’s deed.

## Twenty safeguards before implementation

1. Trace the exact road-read entry point.
2. Trace the exact Heichel Ikar identifier and route.
3. Resolve “MC l” from repository evidence instead of guessing.
4. Search for existing grouping schemas and serializers.
5. Search for existing daily-study/calendar code.
6. Search for Hebrew-date utilities before adding a library.
7. Search for parsha metadata before importing external data.
8. Search for aliyah boundaries in existing Torah sources.
9. Verify whether the project distinguishes Israel and diaspora.
10. Define the day boundary/timezone policy explicitly.
11. Keep calendar calculation pure and testable.
12. Keep UI adaptation separate from calendar logic.
13. Preserve existing grouping behavior for non-Chitas readers.
14. Handle double parshiyos as one weekly seven-aliyah sequence.
15. Handle Yom Tov / Shabbos displacement without pretending the festival reading is the weekly Chitas sedra.
16. Verify a normal week from Sunday through Shabbos.
17. Verify a double-parsha week.
18. Verify an Israel/diaspora divergence week if the app supports both.
19. Read every touched file back after writing and check indentation/module size.
20. Run focused syntax/unit/runtime tests and compare planned behavior with actual output.

## Completion evidence

Completion requires all of the following:

- observed file paths for road-read, grouping, Heichel Ikar, calendar, and Torah text;
- a documented deterministic calculation for date -> parsha -> weekday aliyah;
- implementation through the existing grouping contract;
- focused tests for calendar and grouping behavior;
- readback of every changed file;
- no unresolved critical edge case found by final search.

## Remaining-work ledger

Until the repository trace is complete, source-file names remain deliberately unspecified. Discovery is the next action; implementation is forbidden until the exact call path is known.
